```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
set.seed(258)

plot_cols <- list(
  main        = "#00695c",
  teal        = "#00695c",
  teal_dark   = "#004d40",
  teal_light  = "#e0f2f1",
  blue        = "#c8e6f3",
  blue_soft   = "#eef8fb",
  grey        = "#f5f6f7",
  gray        = "#f5f6f7",
  yellow      = "#fff8e1",
  orange      = "#f9a825",
  text        = "#2f3437",
  muted       = "#667174",
  border      = "#d8dee2",
  code        = "#f3f4f5",
  white       = "#ffffff",
  red         = "#c62828",
  purple      = "#7e57c2"
)

plotly_slide_layout <- function(
  p,
  title = NULL,
  x_title = NULL,
  y_title = NULL,
  width = NULL,
  height = 390,
  x_range = NULL,
  y_range = NULL,
  margin = list(l = 70, r = 25, t = 70, b = 60)
) {
  p |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, font = list(size = 16), x = 0.02),
      width = width,
      height = height,
      margin = margin,
      dragmode = FALSE,
      xaxis = list(
        title = x_title,
        range = x_range,
        fixedrange = TRUE,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      yaxis = list(
        title = y_title,
        range = y_range,
        fixedrange = TRUE,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
      plot_bgcolor = "white"
    ) |>
    config(
      displayModeBar = FALSE,
      displaylogo = FALSE,
      scrollZoom = FALSE,
      doubleClick = FALSE,
      staticPlot = FALSE
    )
}
```

```{=html}
<script>
function resizePlotlyOnSlides() {
  if (!window.Plotly) return;
  document.querySelectorAll(".js-plotly-plot").forEach(function(plot) {
    Plotly.Plots.resize(plot);
  });
}

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
  setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 250);
  setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 750);
  setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 1500);

  if (window.Reveal) {
    Reveal.on("ready", function () {
      setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 300);
    });
    Reveal.on("slidechanged", function () {
      setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 300);
    });
    Reveal.on("fragmentshown", function () {
      setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 300);
    });
    Reveal.on("fragmenthidden", function () {
      setTimeout(resizePlotlyOnSlides, 300);
    });
  }

  window.addEventListener("resize", resizePlotlyOnSlides);
});
</script>
```

```{=html}
<script>
document.addEventListener(
  "click",
  function (event) {
    const solutionButton = event.target.closest(
      ".btn-exercise-solution"
    );

    if (solutionButton) {
      const buttonGroup = solutionButton.closest(
        ".btn-group-exercise-editor"
      );

      if (buttonGroup) {
        buttonGroup.dataset.solutionButtonHtml =
          solutionButton.outerHTML;
      }

      return;
    }

    const startOverButton = event.target.closest(
      '.btn-exercise-editor[aria-label="Start Over"]'
    );

    if (!startOverButton) return;

    const currentSlide = startOverButton.closest("section");

    const buttonGroup = startOverButton.closest(
      ".btn-group-exercise-editor"
    );

    if (!currentSlide || !buttonGroup) return;

    window.setTimeout(function () {
      const solutions = currentSlide.querySelectorAll(
        ".exercise-solution"
      );

      solutions.forEach(function (solution) {
        solution.classList.add("d-none");
      });

      if (
        solutions.length === 0 ||
        buttonGroup.querySelector(".btn-exercise-solution") ||
        !buttonGroup.dataset.solutionButtonHtml
      ) {
        return;
      }

      const holder = document.createElement("div");

      holder.innerHTML =
        buttonGroup.dataset.solutionButtonHtml.trim();

      const restoredButton = holder.firstElementChild;

      if (!restoredButton) return;

      restoredButton.onclick = function () {
        solutions.forEach(function (solution) {
          solution.classList.remove("d-none");
        });

        restoredButton.remove();
      };

      buttonGroup.appendChild(restoredButton);
    }, 0);
  },
  true
);
</script>
```

## Chapter Roadmap {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">10.1 - Multinomial model</span>
Use counts across categories when each observation falls into exactly one group.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">10.2 - Goodness of fit</span>
Compare observed counts to expected counts under a hypothesized probability model.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">10.3 - Assumptions</span>
Check independence and expected cell frequencies before using $\chi^2$.
:::
::::

<br>

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core skill</span>
Turn category probabilities into expected counts.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core tool</span>
Use `chisq.test()` to check the statistic, degrees of freedom, P-value, and expected counts.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Core habit</span>
Interpret the result in context, not just as “reject” or “do not reject.”
:::
::::

---

## Why Categorical Data Need a New Tool

::: {.defbox}
So far, many methods focused on means, variances, or proportions.

In this chapter, the data are often **counts across categories**.

Examples:

- Which app did a student choose?
- Which colour did a customer prefer?
- Which pickup time did an order fall into?
- Which outcome happened in a repeated experiment?
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The question is no longer “What is the average?”  
The question is usually: **Do the observed counts match what the model predicted?**
:::

---

## From Binomial to Chi-square

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
For two categories, one count can be modelled with a binomial distribution.

If $Y_1 \sim Bin(n,p_1)$, then for large $n$,

$$
Z=
\frac{Y_1-np_1}
{\sqrt{np_1(1-p_1)}}
\approx N(0,1)
$$

So,

$$
Z^2 \approx \chi^2_1
$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Pearson's idea</span>

Instead of only checking one binomial count, compare every observed count to its expected count.

For two categories:

$$
Q_1=
\sum_{i=1}^{2}
\frac{(Y_i-np_i)^2}{np_i}
$$

This extends naturally to more than two categories.
:::
:::
::::

---

## 10.1 Multinomial Response Model

::: {.defbox}
A **multinomial response model** applies when each trial results in exactly one of $k$ mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories.

The category probabilities are:

$$
p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_k
$$

with

$$
p_1+p_2+\cdots+p_k=1
$$
:::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Trials</span>
There are $n$ independent and identical trials.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Categories</span>
Each trial lands in one of $k$ possible categories.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Counts</span>
The observed category counts are $Y_1,Y_2,\ldots,Y_k$.
:::
::::

---

## Multinomial Counts

::: {.defbox}
If the model probabilities are $p_1,\ldots,p_k$, the expected count in category $i$ is:

$$
E_i=np_i
$$

The Pearson chi-square statistic is:

$$
Q_{k-1}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}
\frac{(Y_i-np_i)^2}{np_i}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}
\frac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i}
$$

For large enough expected counts,

$$
Q_{k-1}\approx \chi^2_{k-1}
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The statistic gets large when observed counts are far from expected counts.
:::

---

## Example: Streaming App Preference

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.87fr 1.13fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A campus media club asks $n=240$ students which streaming app they would keep if they could keep only one.

The club wants to test whether the four apps are equally preferred.

<br>

| App | Netflix | YouTube | Disney+ | Prime |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Observed count | 88 | 72 | 50 | 30 |

Use $\alpha=0.05$.
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.80em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation</span>

If all four apps are equally preferred:

$$
p_1=p_2=p_3=p_4=\frac14
$$

$$
E_i=np_i=240\left(\frac14\right)=60
$$

$$
\chi^2=
\frac{(88-60)^2}{60}
+
\frac{(72-60)^2}{60}
+
\frac{(50-60)^2}{60}
+
\frac{(30-60)^2}{60}
$$

$$
\chi^2=32.13,\qquad df=4-1=3
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>

$$
H_0:p_1=p_2=p_3=p_4=\frac14
$$

$$
H_a:\text{the four probabilities are not all equal}
$$
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.67em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
Since the P-value is very small, we reject $H_0$. The sample gives strong evidence that the four streaming apps are **not equally preferred**.
:::

::::

---

## Example: Campus Café Drink Preference

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.87fr 1.13fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A campus café wants to know whether three cold drink options are equally preferred by students.

A random sample of $n=180$ student purchases gives:

<br>

| Drink | Iced coffee | Matcha latte | Smoothie |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Observed count | 72 | 64 | 44 |

Use $\alpha=0.05$.
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.80em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation</span>

If all three drinks are equally preferred:

$$
p_1=p_2=p_3=\frac13
$$

$$
E_i=np_i=180\left(\frac13\right)=60
$$

$$
\chi^2=
\frac{(72-60)^2}{60}
+
\frac{(64-60)^2}{60}
+
\frac{(44-60)^2}{60}
$$

$$
\chi^2=6.93,\qquad df=3-1=2
$$

$$
p\text{-value}\approx0.031
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>

$$
H_0:p_1=p_2=p_3=\frac13
$$

$$
H_a:\text{the three probabilities are not all equal}
$$
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.67em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
Since $0.031<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. The sample suggests that the three café drinks are not equally preferred.
:::

::::

## 10.2 Chi-square Test for Goodness of Fit

::: {.defbox}
A **chi-square goodness-of-fit test** checks whether observed category counts agree with a hypothesized probability model.

The hypotheses are:

$$
H_0:
p_1=p_{hyp,1},\;
p_2=p_{hyp,2},\;
\ldots,\;
p_k=p_{hyp,k}
$$

$$
H_a:\text{at least one category probability is different}
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The null hypothesis can say “all categories are equal,” but it can also give unequal hypothesized probabilities.
:::

---

## Goodness-of-Fit Test Statistic

::: {.defbox}
The test statistic is:

$$
\chi^2
=
\sum
\frac{(\text{observed count}-\text{expected count})^2}
{\text{expected count}}
$$

where:

$$
\text{expected count}=np_i
$$

The P-value is the area to the right of the observed $\chi^2$ statistic under a chi-square distribution with:

$$
df=k-1
$$
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
This is always a **right-tail test**. Large $\chi^2$ values mean the observed counts are too far from the hypothesized model.
:::

---

## Example: Campus Food Pickup Slots

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.87fr 1.13fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A campus food hall predicts how mobile pickup orders are distributed across four time slots.

The historical model is:

$$
(0.15,\;0.35,\;0.30,\;0.20)
$$

A random sample of $n=200$ orders gives:

| Slot | 11-12 | 12-1 | 1-2 | 2-3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Observed count | 24 | 82 | 54 | 40 |

Use $\alpha=0.05$.
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.80em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation</span>

Expected counts:

$$
200(0.15,0.35,0.30,0.20)
=
(30,70,60,40)
$$

$$
\chi^2=
\frac{(24-30)^2}{30}
+
\frac{(82-70)^2}{70}
+
\frac{(54-60)^2}{60}
+
\frac{(40-40)^2}{40}
$$

$$
\chi^2=3.86,\qquad df=4-1=3
$$

$$
p\text{-value}\approx0.277
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>

$$
H_0:(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)
=
(0.15,0.35,0.30,0.20)
$$

$$
H_a:\text{at least one probability differs}
$$
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.67em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
Since $0.277>0.05$, we do not reject $H_0$. The observed pickup counts are reasonably consistent with the historical time-slot model.
:::

::::

---

## Example: Phone Case Colour Demand

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.87fr 1.13fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A phone accessory shop expects case colour demand to follow:

$$
(0.30,\;0.25,\;0.25,\;0.20)
$$

for black, clear, blue, and pink cases.

A sample of $n=150$ recent purchases gives:

| Colour | Black | Clear | Blue | Pink |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Observed count | 63 | 28 | 36 | 23 |

Use $\alpha=0.05$.
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.80em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation</span>

Expected counts:

$$
150(0.30,0.25,0.25,0.20)
=
(45,37.5,37.5,30)
$$

$$
\chi^2=
\frac{(63-45)^2}{45}
+
\frac{(28-37.5)^2}{37.5}
+
\frac{(36-37.5)^2}{37.5}
+
\frac{(23-30)^2}{30}
$$

$$
\chi^2=11.30,\qquad df=3
$$

$$
p\text{-value}\approx0.0102
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Interpretation setup</span>

One term of the statistic is especially large:

$$
\frac{(63-45)^2}{45}=7.20
$$

This shows that black case purchases are far above what the model expected.
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.67em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
Since $0.0102<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. The colour demand pattern does not fit the shop's expected distribution well.
:::

::::

## Reading the Chi-square Statistic

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.defbox}
Each category contributes one term:

$$
\frac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i}
$$

The total $\chi^2$ statistic is the sum of these terms.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">How to read the terms</span>

A category contributes more when the observed count is far from the expected count.

This helps explain why the final statistic is small or large.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

observed <- c(Black = 63, Clear = 28,
              Blue = 36, Pink = 23)

expected <- c(45, 37.5, 37.5, 30)

contrib <- (observed - expected)^2 / expected

round(data.frame(
  observed = observed,
  expected = expected,
  contribution = contrib
), 3)
```

---

## 10.3 Sample Size Assumption

::: {.defbox}
The chi-square approximation works well only when the expected counts are large enough.

A common course rule is:

$$
E_i=np_i\ge 5
\quad
\text{for every category}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Good situation</span>

Expected counts:

$$
(30,70,60,40)
$$

Every expected count is at least 5, so the chi-square approximation is reasonable.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Problem situation</span>

Expected counts:

$$
(2.5,4.5,18,25)
$$

Some expected counts are below 5, so the chi-square approximation may be unreliable.
:::
::::

---

## Assumptions for Chi-square Goodness of Fit

::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.72em; line-height: 1.24; padding: 15px 18px; margin-top: 10px;"}
<span class="label">Assumptions</span>

<ul class="assumption-list" style="gap: 10px;">
  <li><strong>Categorical counts:</strong> The data should be counts in mutually exclusive categories.</li>

  <li><strong>One category per trial:</strong> Each observation should fall into exactly one of the possible categories.</li>

  <li><strong>Independent trials:</strong> The trials or observations should be independent.</li>

  <li><strong>Expected cell frequency:</strong> Each expected count should usually be at least 5.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.thinkbox style="font-size: 0.70em; line-height: 1.22; padding: 13px 16px; margin-top: 14px;"}
<span class="label">Course reminder</span>

Check expected counts, not observed counts. A small observed count is not automatically a problem if the expected count condition is satisfied.
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A goodness-of-fit test has five categories. Under $H_0$, the expected counts are:

$$
(8,\;12,\;20,\;4,\;16)
$$

Which statement is best?
:::

- The test is fine because the total sample size is large
- The test is fine because most observed counts are above 5
- [The chi-square approximation is questionable because one expected count is below 5]{.correct data-explanation="The expected cell frequency condition checks expected counts, and here one expected count is 4, which is below 5."}
- The degrees of freedom should be 5

---

## Practice: Food Delivery App Share

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.87fr 1.13fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A student group claims food delivery app choices on campus follow:

$$
(0.10,\;0.20,\;0.30,\;0.20,\;0.20)
$$

A random sample of $n=150$ students gives:

| App | A | B | C | D | E |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Observed count | 12 | 32 | 42 | 36 | 28 |

Test the model at the 1% significance level.
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.80em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 14px 18px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation</span>

Expected counts:

$$
150(0.10,0.20,0.30,0.20,0.20)
=
(15,30,45,30,30)
$$

$$
\chi^2=
\frac{(12-15)^2}{15}
+
\frac{(32-30)^2}{30}
+
\frac{(42-45)^2}{45}
+
\frac{(36-30)^2}{30}
+
\frac{(28-30)^2}{30}
$$

$$
\chi^2=2.27,\qquad df=5-1=4
$$

$$
p\text{-value}\approx0.687
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Decision rule</span>

At the 1% level, reject $H_0$ only if the P-value is less than $0.01$.
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.67em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
Since $0.687>0.01$, we do not reject $H_0$. The observed app choices are consistent with the claimed distribution.
:::

::::

```{webr}
tt
tt$expected
```

## Chapter Summary

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">1. Model the counts</span>
Use a multinomial model when each trial falls into exactly one of $k$ categories.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">2. Build expected counts</span>
Under the null model:

$$
E_i=np_i
$$

These are the counts we would expect if $H_0$ were true.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">3. Compare with $\chi^2$</span>
Use:

$$
\chi^2=\sum\frac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i}
$$

Large values give evidence against $H_0$.
:::
::::

<br>

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Degrees of freedom</span>

$$
df=k-1
$$
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">P-value</span>
Use the right-tail area under the chi-square distribution.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Assumption check</span>
Each expected count should usually be at least 5.
:::
::::

<span class="label">Final takeaway</span>

Goodness-of-fit tests ask whether the observed category counts are close enough to what the null model predicted, allowing for natural sampling variation.
:::
